title: Can pattern matching run in linear time in the LZ77 input size?
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given a valid LZ77 representation of z phrases of a text T of length N and an explicit nonempty pattern P of length m, decides whether P occurs contiguously in T in O(z+m) worst-case time? Self-referencing copy phrases are allowed. Symbols are integers in $\{1,\ldots,(z+m)^c\}$ for a fixed constant c. Use a word RAM with word size $\Theta(\log(N+m+2))$, the operations specified below, and O(z+m) working words. The input is the compressed text and the explicit pattern; all preprocessing is included.
answer_criterion: Give one uniform algorithm with the stated bounds for every valid input, or prove that no such algorithm exists in this model. The output is one yes/no answer. An algorithm linear in the uncompressed text length, or in a potentially larger grammar representation, does not attain this target.
definitions: Each phrase is either one literal symbol or a pair (s,l) instructing the decoder to append l symbols copied sequentially from an earlier starting position s in the text. For a phrase beginning at p, require 1 <= s < p; the copied interval may overlap the phrase being produced. Phrase boundaries and references occupy O(1) words per phrase. No promise of a greedy parse is needed. The RAM has random access, comparisons, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division, and bitwise Boolean operations and shifts on a word at unit cost; arithmetic results are restricted to a word. There is no access to a separately stored decompressed text or precomputed index.
context:
Ordinary pattern matching scans the text and pattern in linear time. That guarantee can be too expensive for compressed input: a short sequence of copy instructions may describe a text many orders of magnitude larger than the representation. Here the algorithm only has to determine whether an occurrence exists, so a large number of matches does not force a large output.

A match can cross phrase boundaries or occur inside a repeated region. For example, a pattern may start near the end of one copied block and finish in the next. Inspecting each phrase in isolation therefore misses valid occurrences. The challenge is to summarize enough boundary and periodicity information while charging only constant total work per input phrase and pattern symbol.

Grammar compression provides an instructive comparison. Linear-time pattern matching is known when the input is a straight-line grammar, but converting an LZ77 representation to an appropriate grammar can increase its size. The existing grammar algorithm therefore does not immediately give linear time measured in z.

The 2025 seminar question explicitly retains the Lempel–Ziv target. This card fixes the decision version, permits self-references, and charges preprocessing. These choices prevent a reporting cost or an uncharged text index from changing the question.
why: This is a basic test of whether computation can follow the compressed input size rather than the size of the object it describes. Settling it would also clarify whether the representation gap between LZ77 and grammars creates an unavoidable algorithmic cost for a fundamental string operation.

progress.text: Gawrychowski gives deterministic O(z(1+log(N/z))+m) time for LZ-compressed occurrence detection, including self-referential parses.
Ganardi and Gawrychowski obtain O(g+m) time when the supplied text representation is a grammar of size g. This resolves the grammar-input version.
Gawrychowski asks whether the Lempel–Ziv version can be solved in time linear in compressed-text size plus pattern length.
